title: Learning Objectives
section: How I Met Each Learning Outcome
text:
How I Met Each Learning Outcome

Sample Size Determination
Through my work on randomisation for clinical trials, I applied mock power calculations and sample size determination for RCTs. This helped me understand Type I and Type II errors and their practical implications in trial design. I learned to balance statistical power with practical constraints such as budget, timeline, and recruitment feasibility.


Statistical Analysis Plan Development
I developed comprehensive analysis plans for multiple consultation projects, specifying primary and secondary outcomes, statistical methods, and approaches for handling missing data. This skill was particularly important for ensuring reproducibility and transparency in research findings.


Formulating Research Questions
I worked closely with clinical researchers to translate their clinical problems into testable statistical hypotheses. This required ensuring that research questions were specific, measurable, and aligned with available data. The job satisfaction survey and heart murmur studies provided excellent opportunities to practice this skill.


Questionnaire Design
I gained experience working with validated instruments like the Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire (MSQ) and contributed to the design of the MurmurQuiz. This taught me about Likert scales, response bias, and validation measures—critical considerations for reliable data collection.


Formulating Study Designs
My contributions to RCT design through randomisation schedules helped me understand the importance of proper study design. I also gained insight into cross-sectional and observational study limitations through the consultation projects.


Communication – Oral and Written
Throughout my internship, I regularly presented findings to multidisciplinary teams and wrote analysis reports that translated complex statistics for clinical audiences. This was perhaps the most frequently exercised skill, as every project required clear communication with non-statistical stakeholders.


Research Ethics
My participation in the Data Safety Committee and completion of Good Clinical Practice (GCP) training deepened my understanding of the Declaration of Helsinki principles in practice. I learned that ethical research practices form the foundation upon which all clinical research must be built.


Data Management
I performed extensive data cleaning in R and managed complex datasets with both hour-level and case-level data structures. Creating reproducible workflows was essential for maintaining data integrity and enabling quality control.


Quality Control
I implemented peer review processes using Excel checklists for QC and ensured regulatory compliance in all outputs. This taught me that producing statistically valid results is only part of the job—communicating them clearly and accurately is equally critical.


Advanced Statistical Programming
I developed R packages for analyses, created automated reporting systems, and implemented complex data transformations and modeling. The Shiny app development project, in particular, challenged me to integrate multiple programming skills to create a production-ready tool.


Collaboration
Working effectively within multidisciplinary teams including clinicians, data managers, and regulatory specialists was a daily requirement. I learned the importance of listening, asking clarifying questions, and finding common ground when technical and clinical perspectives diverged.


Consulting Skills
I led consultation meetings, translated clinical questions into statistical problems, and provided actionable recommendations. The mock consultation from the BC module prepared me well, but real-world consultations taught me that flexibility and patience are just as important as technical expertise.


Leadership Skills
On the job satisfaction survey project, I took ownership of the analysis, managed project timelines, and coordinated with multiple stakeholders. This experience showed me that leadership in biostatistics often means guiding the analytical process while empowering collaborators to make informed decisions.


Statistical Analysis
I applied a wide range of statistical methods including ordinal logistic regression, generalized linear models (GLMs) for the fresh gas flow analysis, and factor analysis. Managing Likert scale data taught me the importance of choosing appropriate methods for the data structure and research question.

The internship demonstrated how interconnected these learning outcomes are in practice. A single project often required simultaneously applying multiple skills—from study design and data management to analysis, communication, and collaboration.
The most important lesson I learned is that technical statistical expertise must be paired with strong soft skills. The ability to communicate clearly, collaborate effectively, and manage projects efficiently is what transforms a statistician into an effective biostatistical consultant.

title: Work Outputs
text:
1. Job Satisfaction Survey Analysis

Project Overview
One of the main statistical consulting projects I worked on during my internship involved analysing a job satisfaction survey among anaesthesia consultants and registrars in South Africa. The purpose of the study was to assess key domains of job satisfaction using the Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire (MSQ). We also wanted to explore how satisfaction, demographic variables, and respondents’ intention to leave their current post were associated.


My Responsibilities
My responsibilities covered the full spectrum of statistical support:

Data Management: Imported raw Excel data into R, cleaned and recoded over sixty variables, with particular attention to managing Likert-scale responses, multi-select questions, and missing values
Psychometric Assessment: Implemented scoring framework for MSQ capturing intrinsic, extrinsic, and general satisfaction domains; assessed internal consistency using Cronbach’s alpha; conducted exploratory factor analysis to examine dimensional structure
Statistical Analysis: Used both parametric and non-parametric methods to compare satisfaction scores between consultants and registrars; employed ordinal logistic regression to model intention to leave as a function of demographic predictors
Reporting: Produced comprehensive demographic tables, publication-quality summary tables, and clear visualizations (histograms, boxplots, and Likert plots)



Key Challenges and Learning
A key outcome of the study was to determine whether factors like age and gender were associated with anaesthesiologists’ intention to leave. I used ordinal logistic regression for this. While the computational aspects in R were familiar, interpreting the results in understandable language proved challenging, particularly since this method was new to me. My supervisor encouraged me to make the findings understandable to clinicians. After several attempts, I learned a valuable lesson: “the job is not complete until you can make it understandable.”


Consultation Meeting Experience
This project involved a meeting with the researcher, their two supervisors, and my internship supervisor. Having completed a mock consultation for my degree’s Biostatistical Consulting module, I felt prepared, but the reality was different. I spent the day expecting questions about the regression or ANOVA results. However, much of the 80-minute meeting focused on stylistic aspects of the report, such as adjusting axis font sizes on graphs or selecting density plots instead of histograms.
This experience exposed me to the realities of working within a multidisciplinary team. I realised that much of my time would be spent refining report details to ensure clarity and acceptability for journal submission, rather than focusing solely on statistical analysis. While this initially felt frustrating, I grew to appreciate the collaborative process of generating new knowledge.


Skills Developed

Project management (weekly goal-setting for data cleaning and analysis)
Independent research on best practices for interpreting ordinal logistic regression
Personal quality control and document tracking
Regular communication with team members to keep project on track

section: 2. Can Anaesthesiology Trainees Distinguish Between Different Heart Murmurs?
text:
2. Can Anaesthesiology Trainees Distinguish Between Different Heart Murmurs?

Project Overview
This cross-sectional study investigated whether anaesthesiology trainees could distinguish between benign and pathologic paediatric heart murmurs using pre-recorded audio clips. The project addressed the ability of anaesthetists to identify pathologic murmurs during pre-operative assessments, which directly affects patient safety and theatre efficiency. Participants completed a 20-question online test (MurmurQuiz) and provided background information relating to their clinical experience.


My Responsibilities

Data Management: Developed a modular, reproducible codebase in R that processed raw quiz results and survey data, performed data cleaning, derived performance classifications, and merged relevant covariates
Descriptive Analysis: Produced visual summaries (boxplots) and descriptive tables to explore patterns in test accuracy across experience-related factors
Regression Modeling: Conducted both univariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses to assess associations between clinical experience and murmur recognition performance
Reporting: Summarized models in well-formatted tables using the gtsummary package, enabling easy interpretation by non-statistical stakeholders



Personal Significance
I found this project particularly rewarding since it had undertones of educational research—the overarching theme was to determine how capable trainees are at doing routine yet incredibly important tasks. Beyond this, the fact that the work was focused on paediatric patients specifically gave me a sense of personal satisfaction knowing that the work I was doing could have real-world impact on quality of care provided to some of our most vulnerable patients.


Skills Developed

Development of modular, reproducible analytical code
Integration of data from multiple sources (quiz performance and demographic surveys)
Application of logistic regression for educational research questions
Creation of stakeholder-friendly reports using modern R packages

section: 3. Analysis of Fresh Gas Flow Rates
text:
3. Analysis of Fresh Gas Flow Rates

Project Overview
The “Analysis of Fresh Gas Flow Rates and its Effect on Consumption and Cost of Inhalational Anaesthetic Agents in a Tertiary Academic Hospital in Pretoria” was both one of the most challenging and impactful projects of my internship. Motivated by the growing recognition of climate change and healthcare’s responsibility to address its environmental footprint, this study aimed to examine current anaesthetic practices—specifically, the use of volatile inhalational agents and nitrous oxide, both notable greenhouse gases.


Data Structure Challenges
Initial data cleaning was challenging due to the large volume of data that needed analysis. The raw dataset had information at various levels: one set at the case level and another at the hour level. To streamline the workflow and align with the study’s objectives, I created two separate datasets—one representing each level—before “mapping” variables between them.
A particular obstacle related to how clinicians were represented in the original files. Instead of having each clinician in a separate column, the data stored all names for a given case in a single cell, separated by commas. To address this, I wrote a script in R that parsed the clinician column, split the names by commas, and assigned each name to a new column.


Statistical Approach
After cleaning and restructuring the data, I matched variables across the two datasets to facilitate analysis—a process familiar from the statistical programming workflows used in clinical trials. The analysis included:

Calculating summary statistics
Generating visualizations
Applying a generalized linear model to account for clinicians who worked on multiple cases



Impact and Insights
This project highlighted the importance of meticulous data cleaning and documentation, as well as the value of robust, reproducible code for complex analyses. Importantly, by identifying patterns in anaesthetic agent usage and their associated costs, the findings offer actionable insights that could help reduce the hospital’s carbon footprint and promote environmentally responsible healthcare practices.


Skills Developed

Advanced data restructuring and manipulation in R
String parsing and data extraction from complex formats
Generalized linear modeling for clustered data
Environmental impact assessment in healthcare settings

4. Randomisation

Overview
As the name suggests, randomisation is a principal component of any Randomised Controlled Trial (RCT). Randomly assigning treatment ensures that a participant’s potential health outcomes do not influence the allocation process. This approach makes the treatment groups comparable on average, even with respect to unmeasured confounders. Consequently, comparing outcomes by assigned group yields an unbiased estimate of the treatment’s causal effect.


My Contribution
Being asked to prepare a randomisation schedule was an exciting opportunity, particularly as the topic had not been covered in depth during my MSc. Completing this task gave me a keen sense of accomplishment, as it marked my first concrete contribution to a clinical trial.


Technical Implementation
An especially interesting aspect was the division of the process into two stages:

Mock Randomisation: Employed a fixed random seed to ensure reproducibility for validation purposes
Final Randomisation: Used a randomly selected seed between 1 and 2 million (excluding the mock seed) to generate the actual allocation sequence

While these were mathematically and programmatically identical, this two-stage process ensured both reproducibility (for quality control) and true randomness (for the actual trial).


Skills Developed

Understanding of different randomisation methods (simple, blocked, stratified)
Programming techniques in R to ensure true randomness
Regulatory procedures for generating and documenting randomisation sequences
Appreciation for the rigour needed in clinical trials

5. Data Safety Committee

Background and Motivation
I am particularly interested in the crucial role that ethics plays in clinical research. Since beginning my journey in public health, I have come to regard ethical research practices as a fundamental part upon which the entire research process is built. I dedicated many hours to understanding the Declaration of Helsinki, the lasting infamy of the Tuskegee Syphilis Study, and the role of safety review committees in clinical trials.


Scigenix’s Commitment to Ethics
This emphasis on ethics became especially clear during my internship at Scigenix. From the start, Scigenix demonstrated a deep commitment to patient wellbeing. I was encouraged to approach the clinical research process holistically, always remembering that our goal is to improve people’s lives. In biostatistics, our work is often far removed from patients—both physically and metaphorically—which can make it easy to forget the individuals behind the numbers and graphs. To address this, the company enrolled all staff in an intensive Good Clinical Practice (GCP) training course.


Data Safety Committee Meeting
One of my goals going into this internship was to attend a Data Safety Review Committee meeting. These committees are tasked with scrutinising clinical trial conduct, evaluating results, and safeguarding patient safety. Although they play an integral role in research, many young biostatisticians perceive them as mysterious, since participating requires substantial clinical trial experience.
While the meeting itself was strictly confidential, I was able to see firsthand that there was zero tolerance for anything that might put study participants at risk. Notably, I found it interesting that decisions on whether to continue a study were made formally through voting.


Learning Outcomes

Understanding of the role and function of Data Safety Monitoring Boards
Appreciation for the ethical responsibilities of biostatisticians
Insight into formal decision-making processes in clinical trials
Reinforcement of patient-centered approach to research

6. Quality Control

The Standard of Excellence
In clinical research, the expectation is that all work produced, whether statistical outputs, tables, figures, or reports, is of the highest standard and as close to flawless as possible. This standard is not simply aspirational but essential, given the regulatory and ethical stakes involved in trial reporting.


QC Process Implementation
To achieve this level of rigour, we employed a structured quality control process grounded in peer review and accountability. Specifically, we used a comprehensive checklist system developed in Excel, where team members took responsibility for reviewing a colleague’s work line by line.
Each item on the checklist targeted a specific aspect of quality:

Correct application of statistical methods
Alignment between R outputs and their presentation in Word
Compliance with pre-specified templates and reporting conventions

No detail was considered too minor to call for attention. Stylistic consistency such as the use of decimal points, abbreviations, and font sizing was meticulously checked. Figures were assessed for readability, clarity, and adherence to visual standards. Even elements like axis labels, colour schemes, and legend placement were scrutinised to ensure they communicated information effectively and professionally.


Insights Gained
This process highlighted the importance of collaborative vigilance and instilled in me a deep respect for the behind-the-scenes discipline that underpins transparent and reproducible research. It also reinforced the notion that producing statistically valid results is only one part of the job—communicating them clearly and accurately is equally critical.

7. Annotated Case Report Forms

Introduction to CDISC Standards
One of the most eye-opening tasks during my internship was working on annotated Case Report Forms (CRFs). Before starting this work, I had only a theoretical understanding of how clinical trial data gets organized and standardized. What I discovered was a world of detail that makes my earlier coursework seem refreshingly straightforward by comparison.


The Task
The basic premise seemed simple enough: take the forms used to collect patient data during clinical trials and figure out where each piece of information should go according to CDISC SDTM (Study Data Tabulation Model) standards. In practice, this meant looking at everything from basic demographic questions to complex adverse event reporting and deciding which standardized “domain” each variable belonged to.


The Complexity
Working through these domain mappings quickly taught me that what appears obvious often is not. A simple question about a patient’s medical history might seem like it clearly belongs in the Medical History (MH) domain, but depending on when it was collected and how it relates to the study, it could potentially fit elsewhere. I found myself constantly referring to CDISC implementation guides, trying to decode the logic behind these classification systems.


Broader Impact
What struck me most about this experience was how it illuminated the incredible infrastructure supporting modern clinical research. Before this internship, I understood clinical trials primarily through the lens of statistical analysis. Working on CRF annotations revealed the enormous effort required just to ensure that data can be collected, organized, and submitted in ways that regulatory agencies can review and approve.
This work also gave me a new appreciation for the tedious regulatory requirements that govern clinical research. What initially appeared to be bureaucratic complications revealed themselves as essential safeguards ensuring that clinical trial data can be trusted, compared across studies, and used to make important decisions about drug safety and efficacy.

title: Work Outputs
text:
8. Manual Edit Checks

Overview
One of the most involved experiences during my internship involved working on the Manual Edit Check (MEC) process for a clinical trial. What initially appeared to be a straightforward data validation exercise quickly revealed itself as a sophisticated quality assurance framework that underpins the integrity of clinical research.


Scope of the MEC Process
The MEC process for the study encompassed 134 unique validation rules spanning the entire clinical data lifecycle. These checks were systematically categorized into:

Clinical (CLIN) checks: Focused on clinical logic and medical plausibility
Listing (LIS) checks: Focused on data completeness and consistency

The checks covered fifty-seven different Case Report Forms across thirty-four visit contexts from initial screening through study completion. The sheer scope of this validation framework was initially overwhelming, particularly given that my earlier exposure to data quality control had been limited to basic data cleaning exercises in coursework.


Technical Implementation
My primary responsibility involved implementing and refining the R-based validation framework that executed these checks automatically. Each validation rule required translation into a dedicated R function that would examine specific data elements and return standardized results:

PASS: Data meeting all criteria
FAIL: Definitive errors requiring correction
REVIEW: Cases demanding manual evaluation and clinical judgment



Complex Validation Logic
The most intellectually stimulating aspect was working with the Inclusion/Exclusion criteria checks, which included thirty of the total validation rules. These checks required sophisticated logic to manage scenarios such as specific medical events during the study period—cases where participants initially meeting eligibility criteria might experience status changes that affected their continued participation.
The cross-form validation components proved particularly challenging, as they demanded integration of data from multiple CRF domains to ensure consistency. For instance, confirming that adverse event onset dates aligned with visit dates required matching temporal data across different forms while accounting for potential data entry variations and protocol-defined visit windows.


Impact on Understanding
Working on this project fundamentally changed my appreciation for the infrastructure supporting clinical research. Before this experience, I understood clinical trials primarily through the lens of statistical analysis and study design. The MEC process revealed the enormous effort needed to ensure that data can be trusted for regulatory submissions—an aspect of biostatistical work that receives little attention in academic coursework but proves essential in practice.

title: Work Outputs
text:
9. Shiny App Development

Project Overview
During the latter phase of my internship, I undertook what would become one of the most technically challenging and professionally rewarding projects: developing a production-grade Shiny application for comparing clinical trial datasets and validating medical coding compliance.


Business Need
This project emerged from a dual need within Scigenix’s quality assurance workflow:

Data Validation: The ability to efficiently validate data consistency across various stages of clinical trial data processing, particularly during database lock procedures that precede regulatory submissions
Coding Compliance: Ensuring accurate medical coding using current MedDRA (Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities) and WHO Drug Dictionary terms



Technical Architecture
The application’s core functionality centred on two complementary validation processes:

Dataset Comparison Module

Implemented using the Arsenal package’s comparedf() function in R
Designed to identify discrepancies that could affect trial integrity
Capable of handling large clinical datasets with multiple data domains



Coding Checks Module

Validates medical terminology across three critical domains:

Adverse Events (AE)
Medical History (MH)
Concomitant Medications (CM)

Ensures all medical terms coded using current dictionary versions
Validates LLT_CURRENCY (Lowest Level Term Currency) to guarantee regulatory compliance with MedDRA standards




Development Approach
My approach to development followed the {golem} framework, an R package that simplifies the creation and deployment of production-ready Shiny apps. I came to appreciate this framework for its emphasis on:

Production readiness
Software development best practices
Modular architecture

I structured the full application using smaller Shiny “modules”—one for data comparison and another for coding checks—a process akin to “eating an elephant bit-by-bit.” The coding module required particular attention to dictionary management, as it needed to interface with multiple MedDRA versions and WHO Drug dictionaries stored on the company’s SharePoint system.


Lessons Learned
Reflecting on this experience, I realize how it synthesized everything I had learned during my MSc while simultaneously exposing me to entirely new domains of knowledge. The project required not just statistical and programming expertise, but also an understanding of:

Clinical research processes
Medical coding standards
Regulatory requirements
Enterprise software development practices

The gap between academic programming and production-grade software became starkly apparent. Where my coursework emphasized getting the right answer, this project demanded getting the right answer reliably, reproducibly, and verifiably, with comprehensive documentation of every decision.


Impact
The most valuable lesson from this project was understanding how biostatisticians can contribute beyond traditional analysis roles. By developing tools that enhance both data quality and coding compliance while streamlining validation processes, we can multiply our impact across entire research programs. This application will save Scigenix several hours per study in data validation and coding verification time while reducing error rates—a tangible contribution to improving clinical research efficiency and regulatory compliance.

Dr. Volmink’s session wove together personal narrative with broader principles of leadership and equity in health research. The leadership discussion was profoundly inspiring, expanding my view of what biostatisticians can achieve beyond technical contributions. The combination of aspirational leadership content with practical conflict management created a realistic picture of senior biostatistical practice. Leadership in biostatistics isn’t about formal authority but about influence through expertise, relationship-building, and commitment to scientific integrity. Conflicts often arise from misaligned expectations or communication failures rather than fundamental disagreements. The discussion on equity revealed how statistical choices—from study design to analysis methods—can either perpetuate or address health disparities.


5. Conclusion
This final day synthesized technical, interpersonal, and ethical dimensions of biostatistical practice, emphasizing that senior practitioners must navigate all three simultaneously. Success requires not just managing conflicts but preventing them through clear communication and aligned expectations.


6. Action Plan
I will identify leadership opportunities within current projects, even without formal authority. title: Week 2, Day 2

The Triangle of Statistical Communication revealed communication as multifaceted—requiring active listening and strategic questioning, not just clear explanations. The ending practices showed how proper closure ensures mutual understanding and commitment to next steps. Observing real consultations allowed us to see the ASCCR framework applied holistically.

The communication triangle validated my suspicion that I’d been over-emphasizing explanation at the expense of listening and questioning. The triangle model effectively balanced different communication modes, preventing over-reliance on any single approach. The relationship emphasis correctly identified it as foundational rather than supplementary. The ending techniques addressed a common weakness—consultations that drift off rather than concluding decisively. Video observation provided insights impossible to gain from description alone.


4. Analysis
Effective statistical communication requires code-switching between technical and lay vocabularies while maintaining precision. Relationship-building in professional contexts differs from social relationships—it requires demonstrating competence, reliability, and genuine interest in collaborators’ success. Proper endings prevent the common problem of misaligned expectations that surface weeks later. The video observations revealed that even experienced practitioners must consciously apply these principles—they don’t become automatic.


5. Conclusion
This day demonstrated that communication and relationship skills are not “soft” additions to technical expertise but fundamental competencies that enable statistical knowledge to create impact. Without these skills, even brilliant statistical insights may fail to influence research or practice.


6. Action Plan
I will practice the “listening-first” approach in my next consultation, consciously waiting before offering solutions. The ASCCR framework successfully integrated previously disparate concepts about collaboration into a coherent model. The POWER structure’s emphasis on explicit time management and expectation-setting addressed common consultation pitfalls. Role-playing, while initially awkward, provided safe space to experiment with different approaches. The Q1Q2Q3 method effectively prevented premature jumping to statistical solutions before fully understanding research contexts.


4. Analysis
The frameworks reveal that effective collaboration is learnable and teachable, not merely a personality trait. The attitude of being “domain-expert centered” represents a fundamental shift from statistics-centered thinking. The POWER structure’s “Reflect” component emphasizes continuous improvement—each consultation becomes a learning opportunity. The practice sessions demonstrated that initial discomfort with structured approaches diminishes rapidly with repetition.


5. Conclusion
This foundational day established that systematic approaches to collaboration can enhance both efficiency and effectiveness. The ASCCR framework provides a mental model for navigating complex collaborative relationships, while the POWER structure offers practical tools for immediate implementation.


6. Action Plan
I will implement the POWER structure in my next three consultations, documenting what works and what needs adaptation. I’ll practice the Q1Q2Q3 approach by retroactively applying it to past projects, identifying where deeper questioning might have led to better outcomes. I’ll also develop a personal “collaboration attitude statement” to review before meetings.

text: Looking back on my three-month internship at Scigenix, I can see how transformative this experience has been for my professional development as a biostatistician. This reflection addresses what I learned, why this learning was significant, what I would have done differently, and the challenges I encountered along the way.

title: Reflection
text:
What Did I Learn?

Technical Skills
The internship solidified and extended my technical statistical knowledge in several ways:
Advanced Data Management My coursework prepared me for analyzing clean datasets, but the internship taught me that data cleaning is often 50-70% of the work. I learned to handle complex data structures (hour-level vs. case-level data), parse messy text fields, and create reproducible data processing pipelines. The fresh gas flow project, in particular, taught me the value of thinking carefully about data structure before diving into analysis.
Production-Grade Programming While I was comfortable with R programming from my coursework, the internship introduced me to software engineering principles for biostatistics. The {golem} framework for Shiny app development, the R package structure for analyses, and the rigorous version control practices at Scigenix showed me what it means to write code that others can trust and maintain years later.
Regulatory Standards Perhaps the most unexpected learning area was the regulatory framework governing clinical research. CDISC standards, MedDRA coding, ICH guidelines—these were barely mentioned in my coursework but proved essential for clinical trial work. Annotating CRFs and developing the coding compliance module gave me practical insight into why these standards exist and how they protect patient safety.


Soft Skills
If I’m honest, the soft skills I developed may prove more valuable than the technical ones:
Communication I learned that explaining statistical concepts clearly is just as important as choosing the right analysis method. The job satisfaction project taught me that “the job is not complete until you can make it understandable.” I practiced translating p-values and confidence intervals into language that clinicians could use to make decisions.
Project Management Managing multiple projects simultaneously, setting weekly goals, tracking deliverables, and coordinating with diverse stakeholders taught me organizational skills that no coursework could provide. I learned to balance perfectionism with pragmatism—knowing when to refine an analysis further and when the current version is good enough to share.
Collaboration The multidisciplinary nature of clinical research means constant collaboration with clinicians, data managers, medical writers, and regulatory specialists. I learned to listen more than I speak, to ask clarifying questions before assuming I understand the problem, and to appreciate that my statistical expertise is just one piece of the puzzle.
Resilience Not every analysis goes smoothly. Data doesn’t always behave as expected. Collaborators sometimes request changes that feel unnecessary. I learned to view setbacks as learning opportunities rather than failures, and to maintain professional composure even when frustrated.

title: Reflection
text:
Why Was This Learning Significant?

Bridging the Theory-Practice Gap
My MSc coursework provided an excellent theoretical foundation, but the internship showed me how to apply that knowledge in messy, real-world situations. Understanding the difference between statistical significance and clinical relevance, between a perfect analysis and a timely one, between what the textbook says and what actually works—these insights are what transform a student into a practitioner.


Understanding the Bigger Picture
Before the internship, I thought about statistics in isolation—choose a test, run it, interpret the results. Now I understand that statistical analysis sits within a complex ecosystem: research ethics, regulatory requirements, patient safety, budget constraints, timeline pressures, and organizational politics. Seeing this broader context has made me a more thoughtful and effective biostatistician.


Career Direction
The internship confirmed that I want to pursue a career in clinical research biostatistics. Seeing the tangible impact of statistical work on patient care—whether through the heart murmur study potentially improving pre-operative assessments or the fresh gas flow analysis contributing to environmental responsibility—gave me a sense of purpose that theoretical coursework couldn’t provide.


Professional Identity
I entered the internship as a student learning biostatistics. I’m leaving as a biostatistician who happens to still be completing formal studies. This shift in identity—from student to professional—may sound subtle, but it has profoundly affected how I approach problems, communicate with colleagues, and think about my career.

title: Reflection
section: What Would I Have Done Differently?
text:
What Would I Have Done Differently?

Earlier Engagement with Medical Terminology
Looking back, I wish I had spent time before the internship familiarizing myself with basic medical terminology and clinical concepts. While I picked up necessary terms quickly during projects, having this foundation from the start would have made initial discussions more efficient and reduced the cognitive load when learning new statistical methods simultaneously.


More Proactive Questions
In the early weeks, I sometimes hesitated to ask questions for fear of appearing incompetent. I now realize that asking clarifying questions early saves time later and demonstrates professional maturity rather than weakness. If I could do it again, I would be more proactive in seeking clarification when project requirements were ambiguous.


Systematic Documentation from Day One
While I maintained good documentation throughout the internship, I wish I had been even more systematic from the beginning. Keeping a daily log of what I learned, challenges I faced, and solutions I discovered would have made this reflection easier to write and would provide valuable reference material for future projects.


Time Management for Reflective Practice
The intensity of project work sometimes meant that reflection happened only when required (like for this portfolio). Building in regular time for reflection—perhaps 30 minutes every Friday afternoon—would have deepened my learning in real-time rather than retrospectively.

title: Reflection
section: Challenges Encountered and How I Handled Them
text:
Challenges Encountered and How I Handled Them

Challenge 1: Imposter Syndrome
The Challenge: Especially in the first month, I felt overwhelmed by how much I didn’t know. Experienced colleagues seemed to navigate complex regulatory requirements and statistical challenges effortlessly, while I struggled with basic concepts like CDISC domains.
How I Handled It: I reminded myself that comparing my beginning to their middle wasn’t fair. I focused on daily progress rather than absolute expertise. I also found that being honest about what I didn’t know—rather than pretending—actually built trust with colleagues who appreciated my willingness to learn.
What I Learned: Everyone was once a beginner. Expertise comes from experience, not from innate talent. Being comfortable with not knowing everything is actually a sign of professional maturity.


Challenge 2: Balancing Multiple Projects
The Challenge: At one point, I was simultaneously working on the job satisfaction analysis, developing the Shiny app, and learning about manual edit checks. The context-switching was exhausting and I worried about doing justice to any single project.
How I Handled It: I implemented time-blocking—dedicating specific days or half-days to specific projects rather than trying to make progress on everything simultaneously. I also communicated more proactively with my supervisor about realistic timelines.
What I Learned: Saying no (or “not yet”) is sometimes the most professional response. Clear communication about capacity prevents over-commitment and under-delivery.


Challenge 3: Technical Obstacles with Real Consequences
The Challenge: When working on the manual edit checks, I encountered validation rules that seemed to produce false positives. Unlike coursework where errors are academic, these errors could delay a clinical trial or, worse, allow invalid data to proceed.
How I Handled It: Rather than assuming my code was correct, I systematically tested edge cases, consulted documentation, and when still uncertain, brought specific examples to senior colleagues for review. I learned to value thoroughness over speed.
What I Learned: In clinical research, being approximately right is not good enough. The stakes—patient safety, regulatory compliance, company reputation—demand precision. This isn’t perfectionism; it’s professionalism.


Challenge 4: Navigating Stakeholder Disagreements
The Challenge: During the job satisfaction project meeting, the researcher and their supervisors had different views on how results should be presented. As the statistician, I was caught in the middle of competing preferences.
How I Handled It: I focused on statistical principles and evidence-based practice rather than personal preferences. I provided options when multiple approaches were defensible, clearly explaining the trade-offs. I remained neutral and professional, positioning myself as an expert advisor rather than an advocate for any particular stakeholder.
What I Learned: The statistician’s role is often to facilitate evidence-based decision-making, not to make decisions unilaterally. Understanding group dynamics and maintaining professional neutrality are important skills.


Challenge 5: The Pace of Industry vs. Academia
The Challenge: I was accustomed to academic timelines where thorough exploration of methods is valued. At Scigenix, project timelines were often tight, and “good enough” sometimes had to suffice when “perfect” wasn’t feasible.
How I Handled It: I learned to prioritize—which aspects of an analysis were critical to get exactly right (e.g., primary outcomes, regulatory requirements) vs. which were less critical (e.g., exploratory subgroup analyses). I also got better at scoping projects realistically upfront.
What I Learned: Perfect is the enemy of good. In industry, delivering a solid analysis on time is more valuable than delivering a perfect analysis too late. This doesn’t mean compromising on quality for core analyses, but it does mean being strategic about where to invest effort.

title: Reflection
text:
Overall Reflections

The Most Important Lesson
If I had to distill the internship into one lesson, it would be this: Biostatistics is fundamentally a people discipline, not just a technical discipline. The statistical methods matter, of course, but success depends on understanding what collaborators need, communicating clearly, managing expectations, and building trust. The best analysis in the world is worthless if you can’t explain it in a way that enables decision-making.


Gratitude
I am deeply grateful to Scigenix for taking a chance on a student with limited practical experience. The supportive culture, excellent mentorship from Dr. Swart and other colleagues, and the diversity of projects I was exposed to exceeded my expectations. The company’s commitment to scientific excellence while maintaining a genuinely enjoyable work environment set a standard I will carry forward in my career.


Looking Forward
As I complete my MSc and look toward my career, the internship has given me clarity about what I want from professional life:

Work that has tangible impact on patient care and public health
Collaborative environments where statistical expertise is valued and integrated into decision-making
Opportunities for continuous learning and technical growth
Organizations that balance scientific rigor with supportive culture

I’m excited to take the skills, knowledge, and professional identity I’ve developed at Scigenix into the next chapter of my career.







Final Thought



This internship has fundamentally shaped how I understand the role of a biostatistician in modern clinical research. It has prepared me not just with technical skills, but with the professional maturity, collaborative mindset, and practical wisdom needed to contribute meaningfully to improving human health through rigorous, ethical, and innovative research.

Detailed Module Connections

Principles of Statistical Inference
The foundational concepts of hypothesis testing, Type I and Type II errors, and statistical power learned in this module were directly applied when determining sample sizes for clinical trials. Understanding the balance between statistical rigor and practical constraints was crucial for making sound recommendations to study sponsors.


Design and Analysis of Clinical Trials
This module provided the theoretical framework for understanding randomized controlled trials, blinding, allocation concealment, and intention-to-treat analysis. My work on randomisation schedules and participation in Data Safety Committee meetings brought these concepts to life, showing me the real-world complexities of implementing theoretically sound trial designs.


Biostatistical Consulting
The most directly relevant module to my internship. The ASCCR framework (Ask, Structure, Communicate, Clarify, Report), LISA Collaborative Attitude, and POWER structure for collaboration meetings were tools I used regularly. The mock consultations we conducted during the module prepared me well for real client interactions, though I quickly learned that actual consultations require even more flexibility and patience than practice sessions suggested.


Fundamentals of Epidemiology
Understanding study designs, bias, confounding, and effect modification from this module was essential for evaluating the research questions posed by collaborators. The cross-sectional studies I worked on (job satisfaction survey, heart murmur recognition) required careful consideration of the limitations inherent in these designs.


Data Management & Statistical Computing
This module’s emphasis on reproducible research, version control, and good programming practices directly influenced how I structured my analytical work at Scigenix. Every project was developed as a self-contained R package, ensuring transparency and reproducibility—principles heavily emphasized in this module.


Linear Models
The regression techniques learned in this module were foundational for the analyses I conducted. Understanding how to interpret regression coefficients, assess model assumptions, and communicate results in plain language was essential for effective consulting.


Categorical Data Analysis & GLMs
This module was particularly relevant for the job satisfaction survey (ordinal logistic regression for intention to leave) and the fresh gas flow analysis (GLMs accounting for repeated measures). Understanding when and how to apply these methods was crucial for producing valid results.


Longitudinal Data Analysis
While I didn’t conduct formal longitudinal analyses during my internship, understanding the concepts of within-subject correlation and appropriate modeling approaches helped me appreciate the complexity of the repeated measures data I encountered in clinical trials.

text:
From Theory to Practice: Key Insights

The Gap Between Clean Textbook Data and Real-World Messiness
My coursework typically provided clean, well-structured datasets designed to teach specific statistical concepts. The internship exposed me to the reality of incomplete data, inconsistent coding, and variables that don’t behave as expected. Data cleaning often took 50-70% of project time—a reality not always emphasized in coursework.


Statistical Significance vs. Clinical Relevance
Theoretical modules teach us to focus on p-values and confidence intervals. Clinical collaborations taught me that statistical significance means little if the effect size isn’t clinically meaningful. Learning to have these conversations with clinicians was one of the most valuable skills I developed.


The Importance of Communication
Technical skills from my modules were necessary but not sufficient. The ability to explain complex statistical concepts in plain language, to listen carefully to collaborators’ concerns, and to ask clarifying questions proved just as important as knowing which test to run.


Reproducibility in Practice
While coursework emphasized reproducibility in principle, the internship showed me what it means in practice: version-controlled code, comprehensive documentation, validation scripts, and standardized workflows. The R package structure used at Scigenix ensured that analyses could be reproduced months or years later—a critical requirement for regulatory submissions.

text:
Gaps and Areas for Further Development

Regulatory Knowledge
While my statistical training was solid, I realized that understanding regulatory requirements (ICH guidelines, FDA regulations, CDISC standards) is essential for clinical trial work. This is an area where additional formal training would be valuable.


Software Engineering Practices
The Shiny app development project exposed gaps in my knowledge of software engineering principles like unit testing, continuous integration, and deployment. These skills are increasingly important for biostatisticians developing analytical tools.


Medical Terminology
Better familiarity with medical terminology and clinical concepts would have made initial project discussions more efficient. While I picked up relevant terms quickly, a more systematic foundation would have been helpful.







Key Takeaway



The internship demonstrated that the MSc Biostatistics curriculum provides an excellent theoretical foundation, but real-world consulting requires integrating knowledge across modules while developing soft skills like communication, project management, and collaboration. The greatest value came from applying multiple modules’ concepts simultaneously to solve complex, messy real-world problems.

title: Introduction & Background
text:
Background of Organisation
Scigenix is a dynamic clinical research organization that specializes in data-driven solutions for the pharmaceutical and healthcare sectors. With a global team of experts, the company brings together a wide range of skills, including data science, biostatistics (the application of statistics to biological and health-related research), data management, and medical writing. Its strength lies in leveraging open-source technologies to deliver cost-effective, precise, and scalable solutions across the full spectrum of clinical research—from the initial study design to the final steps of regulatory submission, which is the formal process of submitting research findings to health authorities for review and approval.
The organization positions itself as a change-maker in the clinical research world, particularly in addressing challenges related to data collection, cleaning, analysis, and reporting under strict regulatory constraints. These constraints are guidelines and requirements set up by authorities to regulate the conduct of research. If not addressed effectively, such challenges can lead to delayed drug approvals and substantial financial losses for sponsors. Scigenix fills this gap by offering streamlined, AI-supported data processing and analysis pipelines that support faster, higher-quality decision-making.
Beyond technical capabilities, Scigenix is defined by its strong internal culture and values. These include scientific excellence, attention to detail, client-centricity, a collaborative spirit, and a supportive work environment.
In the biostatistics unit where I was placed, R is the primary programming language used for analysis and reporting. Each project is structured as a self-contained software solution, often in the form of an R package. An R package is a collection of code and documentation that standardizes analysis workflows, ensuring consistency and reproducibility in research findings. This approach allows for transparency and good software development practices. The biostatistics unit supports all phases of clinical research, with a particular emphasis on robust statistical methodologies, clear documentation, and regulatory compliance.
Scigenix’s long-term vision is to become a transformative force in the clinical research industry, especially as an advocate for open-source solutions, while keeping its commitment to quality, accessibility, and innovation.

The Scigenix office is based in a converted home in Hazelwood, Pretoria—a residential area that has, in recent years, transformed into a cosmopolitan neighbourhood filled with new offices, shops, and restaurants.
